full_citation: Saeed, M., Mohamed, E., Mohamed, M., Raza, S., Abdul-Mageed, M., & Shehata, S. (2024). Desert Camels and Oil Sheikhs: Arab-Centric Red Teaming of Frontier LLMs. arXiv:2410.24049.
models_or_system: GPT-4, GPT-4o, Llama 3.1 8B and 405B, Mistral 7B, Claude 3.5 Sonnet
population_categories: Arabs vs Westerners (pooled groups)
manipulation: Bias dataset across 8 domains (e.g., women's rights, terrorism, anti-Semitism) plus jailbreak prompts exaggerating negative traits
outcome: Share of responses biased against Arabs; jailbreak attack success rate
main_result: Negative bias toward Arabs in 79% of cases; Llama 3.1-405B most biased; GPT-4o most jailbreak-vulnerable; all models except Claude above 87% attack success in three categories; Claude still biased in 7 of 8 categories
limitations: Arab treated as one pooled category; stereotype/safety framing, no allocative decision; preprint (no peer-reviewed version found via Crossref)
relation_to_project: Establishes pooled anti-Arab bias in frontier LLMs; motivates asking whether the pooled 'Arab' estimate hides between-country heterogeneity
novelty_threat_reason: Pooled Arab-vs-West comparison in a red-teaming setting; no national-origin variation, no hiring decision

full_citation: Saeed, M. Y. G., Abdul-Mageed, M., & Shehata, S. (2026). Surfacing Subtle Stereotypes: A Multilingual, Debate-Oriented Evaluation of Modern LLMs. In Proceedings of the Language Resources and Evaluation Conference (LREC 2026), pp. 8106-8121. arXiv:2511.01187.
population_categories: Demographic groups incl. Arabs, Africans, Western groups; 7 languages (English, Chinese, ..., Swahili, Nigerian Pidgin)
manipulation: 8,400 structured debate prompts in 4 domains (Women's Rights, Backwardness, Terrorism, Religion)
outcome: Which group is assigned the stereotyped vs modern role
main_result: Arabs linked to Terrorism and Religion in >=89% of cases; Africans to 'backwardness' (up to 77%); bias grows in lower-resource languages
limitations: Arab pooled; generative role assignment, not decisions about individuals
relation_to_project: Shows which associations (conflict, religion) are most salient for 'Arab'; informs exploratory text flags (mentions_conflict, mentions_religion)
novelty_threat_reason: Group-level stereotype benchmark; no national-origin disaggregation, no hiring

full_citation: Naous, T., Ryan, M. J., Ritter, A., & Xu, W. (2024). Having Beer after Prayer? Measuring Cultural Bias in Large Language Models. In Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the ACL (Volume 1: Long Papers), pp. 16366-16393.
population_categories: Arab vs Western cultural entities (names, foods, etc.)
manipulation: CAMeL: 628 naturally occurring prompts, 20,368 entities across 8 types contrasting Arab and Western culture
outcome: Story generation, NER, sentiment, text-infilling behaviour
main_result: Models favour Western-associated entities in Arabic contexts; stereotyping and cultural unfairness; common Arabic pre-training corpora (e.g., Wikipedia) may be unsuitable for culturally aware LMs
limitations: Entity-level cultural bias in Arabic-language tasks; not national origin of persons; no decisions
relation_to_project: Seed verified. Arab-vs-West cultural default; a different construct from our German-context English CV audit
novelty_threat_reason: Cultural entity bias, pooled Arab culture; not hiring, not nationality-level

full_citation: Abid, A., Farooqi, M., & Zou, J. (2021). Persistent Anti-Muslim Bias in Large Language Models. In Proceedings of the 2021 AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society (AIES '21), pp. 298-306.
population_categories: Religious groups (Muslims vs other religions)
manipulation: Prompt completion, analogical reasoning, story generation; adversarial positive-adjective prompts
main_result: 'Muslim' analogised to 'terrorist' in 23% of test cases; adding the 6 most positive adjectives reduced violent completions for Muslims from 66% to 20%, still above other religious groups
limitations: Religion, not nationality; GPT-3 era; not decisions
relation_to_project: Seed verified. Arab is not Muslim, but religion is a plausible channel of the nationality signal (hence mentions_religion flag). Also early evidence that prompt-level counter-signals only partly mitigate bias (RQ3)
novelty_threat_reason: Different attribute (religion) and task

full_citation: Zahraei, P. S., Tur, G., Hakkani-Tur, D., & Asgari, E. (2025). The Alignment Veto: How Safety Training Suppresses Cultural Knowledge in LLMs [v1 title: 'I Am Aligned, But With Whom? MENA Values Benchmark for Evaluating Cultural Alignment and Multilingual Bias in LLMs', authors Zahraei & Asgari]. arXiv:2510.13154.
models_or_system: 26 models (v2); diverse open and closed models
population_categories: 16 MENA countries: Algeria, Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Libya, Mauritania, Morocco, Palestine, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Sudan, Tunisia, Turkey (14 Arab League members + Iran + Turkey)
manipulation: Perspective framing (neutral / personalised / cultural observer) x language (English vs Arabic, Persian, Turkish); items from WVS-7 and Arab Opinion Index 2022
sample_size: 864 questions (v1); 1.53M human survey responses as reference (v2)
outcome: Alignment of model answers (and first-token logit distributions) with country-level human survey distributions; refusals
main_result: Country-level inequity: Algeria worst-served, Palestine best-served (about 19.8% gap); under Arabic prompting models collapse Arab countries into a single cluster while Iran and Turkey stay separate; internal logits align better with surveys than generated answers ('alignment veto')
limitations: Measures value alignment, not treatment of individuals; no allocative decision; preprint with substantially changed v2
relation_to_project: Strongest evidence that LLM behaviour differs across individual Arab countries AND that models homogenise Arab nations; direct motivation for our within-Arab estimand in a hiring setting
novelty_threat_reason: Already studies country-level heterogeneity across 14 Arab states (for cultural alignment), so 'within-Arab heterogeneity' per se is not new; our contribution must be framed as person-level allocative decisions under a counterfactual design

full_citation: Aly, R., Allam, Y., Gaber, R., & Basta, C. (2025). ArGAN: Arabic Gender, Ability, and Nationality Dataset for Evaluating Biases in Large Language Models. In Proceedings of the 6th Workshop on Gender Bias in NLP (GeBNLP), pp. 256-267.
models_or_system: Llama 3.3, DeepSeek V3, GPT-4o, Aya, JAIS
population_categories: Gender (2), ability (abled/disabled), 20 nationalities referenced in Modern Standard Arabic (including 'Arabs' and 'Egyptians')
manipulation: Bias-revealing sentence-construction prompts in MSA with demographic descriptors
outcome: Identity-attack and toxicity scores (Perspective API), regard/sentiment, gender bias scores; human evaluation
main_result: All models show the same pattern: most negativity toward Arabs, Egyptians, Mexicans and Indians; most positivity toward Americans, Germans and Japanese
limitations: Stereotype generation in Arabic, not decisions; nationality set mixes 'Arabs' with individual nationalities; short workshop paper
relation_to_project: Seed check: ArGAN EXISTS (GeBNLP 2025). Shows nationality-level differentiation incl. an individual Arab nationality (Egyptian) in Arabic-language generation
novelty_threat_reason: Arabic-language stereotype dataset; not hiring, not a within-Arab design

full_citation: Elsafoury, F., & Hartmann, D. (2025). Out of Sight Out of Mind, Out of Sight Out of Mind: Measuring Bias in Language Models Against Overlooked Marginalized Groups in Regional Contexts. arXiv:2504.12767.
population_categories: 270 marginalized groups from Egypt, the remaining 21 Arab countries, Germany, the UK and the US; MSA vs Egyptian Arabic
manipulation: Offensive-stereotyping bias probes; dialect vs MSA comparison
main_result: Higher bias against many marginalized than dominant groups; Arabic LMs show high bias against both marginalized and dominant groups for religion and ethnicity; higher bias measured in Egyptian Arabic than MSA
limitations: Targets within-country marginalized groups, not national origin of applicants; no decision task
relation_to_project: Covers all 22 Arab countries at group level; shows measured bias depends on language variety
novelty_threat_reason: Different construct (in-country marginalized groups) and no hiring

full_citation: Keleg, A. (2025). LLM Alignment for the Arabs: A Homogenous Culture or Diverse Ones? In Proceedings of the 3rd Workshop on Cross-Cultural Considerations in NLP (C3NLP 2025), pp. 1-9.
population_categories: Arab world
manipulation: n/a
main_result: Argues that the assumption that Arabs share one culture is invalid yet widely adopted in multilingual and Arabic-specific LLM development
relation_to_project: Conceptual anchor for disaggregating 'Arab' into national origins
novelty_threat_reason: Makes the homogeneity critique conceptually, so we cannot claim the critique itself as new; no empirical hiring test

full_citation: Almheiri, S., Elbadry, R., Attia, M., Wang, C., Nakov, P., Baldwin, T., & Koto, F. (2025). Cross-Cultural Transfer of Commonsense Reasoning in LLMs: Evidence from the Arab World. In Findings of the ACL: EMNLP 2025, pp. 4593-4614.
models_or_system: Multilingual LLMs; ICL, DITTO, SFT, DPO
population_categories: 13 Arab countries (culturally grounded commonsense items)
manipulation: Lightweight alignment with in-country, cross-country and out-of-region demonstrations
main_result: 12 culture-specific examples from one country improve performance in other Arab countries by about 10% on average
relation_to_project: Evidence that models represent Arab countries as partly distinct but related
novelty_threat_reason: Capability evaluation, not fairness or hiring

full_citation: Asseri, B., Abdelaziz, E., & Al-Wabil, A. (2025). Prompt Engineering Techniques for Mitigating Cultural Bias Against Arabs and Muslims in Large Language Models: A Systematic Review. arXiv:2506.18199.
population_categories: Arabs and Muslims
manipulation: Prompt-based mitigation (cultural prompting, affective priming, self-debiasing, multi-step pipelines, continuous prompts)
main_result: All approaches show some reduction; structured multi-step pipelines up to 87.7% reduction; evidence base very small
limitations: Self-described incomplete; small corpus; no hiring studies
relation_to_project: RQ3: almost no Arab-specific evidence on instruction-based mitigation in decisions
novelty_threat_reason: Review, and it documents the gap

full_citation: Shahid, M. (2026). Computational Orientalism: Measuring Structural Discourse Bias in Large Language Models Using the Middle East Cultural Sensitivity Score (MECSS). arXiv:2608.18100.
population_categories: Middle East (region-level discourse)
manipulation: Conversations about the Middle East scored on 7 Orientalist operations (MECSS)
main_result: Both models reproduce Orientalist framing through structural positioning; introduces 'Said-washing': disclaiming generalisation, then reproducing the structure disclaimed
limitations: Single-author preprint; two models; discourse, not decisions
relation_to_project: E: a Middle-East-specific named form of principle-behaviour inconsistency
novelty_threat_reason: Names a disclaimer-vs-behaviour gap, weakening any claim that such a gap is a new concept

full_citation: Venkit, P. N., Gautam, S., Panchanadikar, R., Huang, T.-H., & Wilson, S. (2023). Nationality Bias in Text Generation. In Proceedings of the 17th Conference of the European Chapter of the ACL (EACL 2023), pp. 116-122.
population_categories: Demonyms of 193 countries
manipulation: Prompt '<Demonym> people are'; 100 stories per demonym; adversarial triggering as debiasing
main_result: Stronger negative bias for countries with fewer internet users and lower economic status; the five most negative demonyms were Libya, Sierra Leone, Sudan, Tunisia, South Sudan (three Arab League members); adversarial triggering reduced bias
limitations: GPT-2; story sentiment, not decisions; no within-Arab analysis
relation_to_project: Seed verified. Early evidence that individual Arab demonyms are treated very differently (Libya/Sudan/Tunisia among the most negative)
novelty_threat_reason: Many-country variation but generation sentiment only, old model, no hiring

full_citation: Zhu, S., Wang, W., & Liu, Y. (2024). Quite Good, but Not Enough: Nationality Bias in Large Language Models - A Case Study of ChatGPT. In Proceedings of LREC-COLING 2024, pp. 13489-13502.
population_categories: 195 countries; Chinese and English prompts
manipulation: 3 prompt types x 4 temperatures x 2 languages
outcome: Automated metrics; expert and ChatGPT pairwise annotations
main_result: Mostly positive output, but negative when prompted with negative inclinations; ChatGPT judges its own text neutral yet shows 'self-awareness' of nationality bias under the same pairwise annotation framework; differences across languages
limitations: Descriptive generation, not decisions; one model
relation_to_project: Seed verified. The neutral-self-rating vs pairwise-detected-bias contrast is a say-do-type discrepancy relevant to E
novelty_threat_reason: Generation-level nationality bias; no hiring, no within-Arab estimand

full_citation: Kamruzzaman, M., Shovon, M. M. I., & Kim, G. L. (2024). Investigating Subtler Biases in LLMs: Ageism, Beauty, Institutional, and Nationality Bias in Generative Models. In Findings of the ACL: ACL 2024, pp. 8940-8965.
population_categories: Age, beauty, institution, nationality (countries grouped e.g. by GDP)
manipulation: Template sentence-completion: pick attribute for group, and reverse direction
outcome: Association between group and positive/negative attributes
main_result: Reports general sentiment biases along less-studied dimensions, including nationality
relation_to_project: Seed verified; background for nationality as an under-studied axis
novelty_threat_reason: Template associations, not hiring

full_citation: Kamruzzaman, M., & Kim, G. L. (2024). Exploring Changes in Nation Perception with Nationality-Assigned Personas in LLMs. arXiv:2406.13993.
population_categories: 193 nationality personas evaluating countries
manipulation: Persona assignment
main_result: All model-persona combinations favour Western European nations; personas favour their own region; Eastern European, Latin American, African nations rated more negatively
limitations: Country perception, not applicant decisions; preprint
relation_to_project: Country-level evaluation heterogeneity exists in LLMs; supports expecting between-country variance
novelty_threat_reason: Not hiring; not within-Arab

full_citation: Manvi, R., Khanna, S., Burke, M., Lobell, D. B., & Ermon, S. (2024). Large Language Models are Geographically Biased. In Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2024), PMLR 235, pp. 34654-34669.
population_categories: Locations worldwide
manipulation: Zero-shot geospatial ratings on objective and subjective topics
outcome: Ratings vs ground truth; bias score
main_result: Ratings correlate with ground truth (Spearman up to 0.89) but are biased against lower-SES locations (e.g., most of Africa) on attractiveness, morality and intelligence (Spearman up to 0.70); bias varies across LLMs
relation_to_project: Suggests an exploratory moderator: within-Arab effects may track country wealth (e.g., GCC vs others)
novelty_threat_reason: Geographic ratings, not hiring

full_citation: Jha, A., Mostafazadeh Davani, A., Reddy, C. K., Dave, S., Prabhakaran, V., & Dev, S. (2023). SeeGULL: A Stereotype Benchmark with Broad Geo-Cultural Coverage Leveraging Generative Models. In Proceedings of ACL 2023 (Volume 1: Long Papers), pp. 9851-9870.
population_categories: Identity groups spanning 178 countries
manipulation: LLM-generated stereotype candidates validated by globally diverse raters
main_result: Broad-coverage stereotype resource; in-region and North-American annotators differ in which stereotypes they recognise
relation_to_project: Possible source for mapping stereotype content of individual Arab nationalities (mechanism, exploratory)
novelty_threat_reason: Benchmark resource

full_citation: Salinas, A., Shah, P. V., Huang, Y., McCormack, R., & Morstatter, F. (2023). The Unequal Opportunities of Large Language Models: Examining Demographic Biases in Job Recommendations by ChatGPT and LLaMA. In Proceedings of EAAMO '23.
population_categories: 20 nationalities generated by asking ChatGPT for 'common nationalities' (incl. Jordan as the only Arab country; also Mexico, Pakistan, India, China, Germany, ...) x 2 gender identities; US baseline with no nationality
manipulation: Templates implying the person may have to return to <COUNTRY> if no job is found
sample_size: e.g., 100 generations per country per prompt (50 he / 50 she); >2,000 generations per analysis
main_result: Consistent deviations for Mexican workers (low-paying jobs, lowest median salary); the no-nationality baseline is itself an outlier vs all nationalities
limitations: Job recommendation, not screening; one Arab country; nationality set chosen by ChatGPT (Western-skewed, no African countries); US frame
relation_to_project: Seed verified. Closest design analog for many-nationality variation with a no-nationality control (mirrors our not_stated condition); its baseline-outlier finding warns that 'no nationality' is not a neutral reference
novelty_threat_reason: Varies many nationalities in an employment-advice task but includes only one Arab country and no screening decision

full_citation: Forcada Rodriguez, E., Perez-de-Vinaspre, O., Campos, J. A., Klakow, D., & Gautam, V. (2025). Colombian Waitresses y Jueces canadienses: Gender and Country Biases in Occupation Recommendations from LLMs. In Proceedings of the 6th Workshop on Gender Bias in NLP (GeBNLP), pp. 182-194.
population_categories: 25 countries (incl. Morocco and Saudi Arabia) x 4 pronoun sets; prompts in English, Spanish, German
manipulation: Systematic variation of country and gender in occupation-recommendation prompts
main_result: Significant gender and country biases; intersectional biases persist even when single-axis parity holds; prompt language matters; instruction-tuned models least biased
limitations: Recommendation, not screening; only two Arab countries
relation_to_project: German-language prompts and multi-country design; confirms country-level variation in occupational framing
novelty_threat_reason: Two Arab countries in a recommendation task; no within-Arab estimand

full_citation: Geiger, R. S., O'Sullivan, F., Wang, E., & Lo, J. (2025). Asking an AI for salary negotiation advice is a matter of concern: Controlled experimental perturbation of ChatGPT for protected and non-protected group discrimination on a contextual task with no clear ground truth answers. PLOS ONE, 20(2), e0318500.
population_categories: Gender (pronouns), 50 US universities (incl. fictional), 19 majors; employee vs employer voice
manipulation: Controlled perturbation of salary-negotiation prompts
main_result: Significant gender gaps (smaller than for other attributes); largest gaps between model versions and between employee- vs employer-voiced prompts; university/major effects inconsistent across versions
relation_to_project: SEED CORRECTION: this study does NOT vary nationality (US universities only, per the paper). Useful only for model-version instability and prompt-voice sensitivity
novelty_threat_reason: No nationality factor

full_citation: Sorokovikova, A., Chizhov, P., Eremenko, I., & Yamshchikov, I. P. (2025). Surface Fairness, Deep Bias: A Comparative Study of Bias in Language Models. In Proceedings of the 6th Workshop on Gender Bias in NLP (GeBNLP), pp. 206-227.
models_or_system: Claude 3.5 Haiku, GPT-4o Mini, Qwen 2.5 Plus, Mixtral 8x22B, Llama 3.1 8B
population_categories: Persona sex; ethnicity (Asian, Black, Hispanic, White); migrant type (expatriate, migrant, refugee)
manipulation: Pre-prompted personae on MMLU; grading user answers; salary negotiation advice
main_result: Negligible MMLU differences; grading shows more bias; salary advice shows pronounced bias (e.g., expatriates higher, refugees lower)
relation_to_project: SEED CORRECTION: does NOT vary nationality. Relevant only because migration-status framing (refugee) may be part of what some Arab nationality signals evoke (e.g., Syrian, Yemeni, Sudanese)
novelty_threat_reason: No nationality factor

full_citation: Pelosio, G., Batra, D., Bovey, N., Hankache, R., Iglesias, C., Cowan, G., & Khraishi, R. (2025). Obscured but Not Erased: Evaluating Nationality Bias in LLMs via Name-Based Bias Benchmarks. arXiv:2507.16989.
models_or_system: OpenAI, Google, Anthropic models (e.g., GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Claude Haiku, Claude Sonnet)
population_categories: BBQ nationality items; explicit nationality labels replaced by culturally indicative names
manipulation: Label-to-name substitution
main_result: Smaller models more biased and less accurate; after substituting names, GPT-4o retains 68% and GPT-4o-mini 76% of the ambiguous-context error rate
relation_to_project: Explicit label vs implicit cue: bias persists across cue types; our design uses the explicit label
novelty_threat_reason: QA benchmark

full_citation: Mao, Y., & Zhao, Y. (2025). Digital Gatekeepers: Exploring Large Language Model's Role in Immigration Decisions. arXiv:2506.21574.
population_categories: Country of origin: Germany, France, Mexico, Philippines, Poland, China, Sudan, Somalia, Iraq, India (Hainmueller & Hopkins 2015 levels); plus gender, education, language, profession, etc.
manipulation: Discrete choice experiment (pairs of immigrant profiles for US admission) + in-depth interviews with the models
main_result: Most country-of-origin coefficients not significant; slight preference for female applicants; in interviews models say country of origin matters less, yet give origin-based judgments (favour Germany/France; suggest 'additional scrutiny' for Iraq, Sudan, Somalia)
limitations: Immigration admission (US), not hiring; only 3 Arab League states; preprint; country levels inherited from a 2015 human conjoint
relation_to_project: Only LLM decision study found that includes several individual Arab League origins, and it pairs revealed choices with stated principles (close to our RQ1 + principle probe)
novelty_threat_reason: Person-level allocative decision with multiple origins incl. Iraq, Sudan, Somalia and a stated-vs-revealed contrast; but not hiring, no within-Arab heterogeneity analysis, few Arab levels

full_citation: Nguyen, I., Suresh, H., Monroe-White, T., & Shieh, E. (2026). Representational Harms in LLM-Generated Narratives Against Global Majority Nationalities. In Proceedings of the 2026 ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency (FAccT '26), pp. 7107-7126.
population_categories: National origin identities (Global Majority vs dominant)
manipulation: Open-ended narrative prompts with national-origin cues; US vs non-US cue swaps
main_result: Minoritised national identities under-represented in power-neutral stories and over-represented in subordinated portrayals (>50x more likely than dominant portrayals); amplified by US cues
relation_to_project: National origin as an under-audited axis; representational harms may underlie allocative gaps
novelty_threat_reason: Narratives, not hiring decisions

full_citation: Lippens, L. (2024). Computer says 'no': Exploring systemic bias in ChatGPT using an audit approach. Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans, 2(1), 100054.
venue: Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans
population_categories: 9 ethnic identities signalled by names: Arab, Asian, Black American, Central African, Dutch, Eastern European, Hispanic, Turkish, White American; x gender
manipulation: Correspondence-audit CV screening; name swaps on otherwise identical CVs across vacancies
main_result: Ethnic discrimination more pronounced than gender discrimination; minority-named applicants (incl. Arab and Turkish) penalised relative to Dutch-named ones; larger in jobs with favourable conditions or higher language demands
limitations: Single model; 'Arab' is one pooled name category drawn from several name sources; names bundle ethnicity, religion, gender; Dutch/Belgian framing
relation_to_project: Closest LLM hiring audit: same paradigm, but treats Arab as ONE category - exactly the pooling our design tests
novelty_threat_reason: Same correspondence-audit paradigm with Arab and Turkish groups; our novelty rests on disaggregating Arab into 22 national-origin signals via an explicit nationality field

full_citation: Huijzer, W., & Chen, J. (2025). Discrimination by LLMs: Cross-lingual Bias Assessment and Mitigation in Decision-Making and Summarisation. arXiv:2509.09735.
population_categories: Backgrounds: Dutch, Turkish, Moroccan, Mexican, European-American, African-American; gender; age; English and Dutch
manipulation: Tamkin et al. (2023) decision templates translated to Dutch; explicit vs name-based salience; 6 decision instructions incl. new mitigation instructions
outcome: P(yes) in decisions; bias in summaries
main_result: Both models biased in decisions (favouring female, younger, and e.g. African-American background); summarisation largely unbiased; best mitigation instruction reduced the max-min group gap by 27% on average; GPT-4o showed reduced bias for all English prompts
limitations: Generic decision scenarios (not a CV audit); only one Arab-League origin (Moroccan); short preprint
relation_to_project: Closest precedent for RQ3 (instruction-based mitigation) with several national-origin backgrounds incl. Moroccan and Turkish in a European setting
novelty_threat_reason: Mitigation + origin backgrounds, but not hiring-specific and no within-Arab comparison

full_citation: Phutane, M., Jung, H., Kim, M. J., et al. (2025). ABLEIST: Intersectional Disability Bias in LLM-Generated Hiring Scenarios. arXiv:2510.10998.
models_or_system: Six LLMs (incl. Claude-3.7 Sonnet, GPT-4.1, Llama-3.1-8B, DeepSeek-chat)
population_categories: Disability x gender x nationality (American, Indian) x caste (Brahmin, Dalit)
manipulation: Generated hiring conversations for varied candidate profiles
main_result: Substantial increases in ableist and intersectional harms toward disabled candidates, often not detected by existing tools
limitations: Nationality has only two levels (US, India)
relation_to_project: Shows 'nationality' in hiring audits often means a US/India contrast, not many origins
novelty_threat_reason: Two nationalities, no Arab origins

full_citation: Javines Bilon, X. (2025). Sociodemographic biases in employment decision-making by large language models: experimental evidence from ChatGPT simulations. Journal of Decision Systems, 34(1).
models_or_system: ChatGPT (3 model versions, 3 temperatures) [per search-engine snippet of the abstract; not read directly]
population_categories: Age, gender, sexuality, national origin [levels not verified]
manipulation: Full factorial resume variation, 2 job types [snippet]
main_result: Snippet reports older and non-U.S. applicants received lower scores; NOT verified against the article
limitations: Publisher page inaccessible (403); national-origin levels unknown
relation_to_project: Potential national-origin hiring audit; must be read before the paper cites it
novelty_threat_reason: Appears to contrast US vs non-US origins; if it disaggregates Arab countries the threat would rise - verify full text

full_citation: Rao, P. S. B., Venkatesan, L. N., Cherubini, M., & Jayagopi, D. B. (2025). Invisible Filters: Cultural Bias in Hiring Evaluations Using Large Language Models. Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society, 8(3), 2164-2176.
population_categories: UK vs Indian job seekers; names varied by gender, caste, region within Indian set
manipulation: Scoring of real interview transcripts; controlled name substitutions
main_result: Indian transcripts scored consistently lower even when anonymised, linked to linguistic features; name substitutions alone had no significant effect
limitations: Cross-national difference arises from transcript language, not a nationality signal
relation_to_project: Caution: name-only manipulations can show nulls; our explicit nationality field is a stronger, more transparent cue
novelty_threat_reason: UK vs India; no Arab origins

full_citation: Leininger, C., Veit, H., Assenmacher, M., & Bender, A. (2026). Fairness Beyond Anonymization? Demographic Leakage in German LLM-Generated Resumes. arXiv:2609.22188 (BIAS 2026 workshop at ECML PKDD).
population_categories: Gender- and ethnicity-associated names (German vs Turkish, per paper HTML snippet)
manipulation: LLM résumé generation from anonymised German job-matching profiles; then anonymisation and leakage classifiers
outcome: Recoverability of gender/ethnicity from generated résumés
main_result: Gender reliably recoverable even after anonymisation (subtle word-choice differences in German); ethnicity leakage weak
limitations: Generation/leakage, not screening decisions; no Arab origins
relation_to_project: German labour-market LLM study using Turkish as the migrant-origin category; supports Turkish benchmark choice
novelty_threat_reason: No Arab origins, no screening decision

full_citation: Tan, B. C. Z., Khoo, S., Doan, B. N., Liu, Z., Chen, N. F., & Lee, R. K.-W. (2026). Small Changes, Big Impact: Demographic Bias in LLM-Based Hiring Through Subtle Sociocultural Markers in Anonymised Resumes. arXiv:2603.05189 (EMNLP 2026).
population_categories: Singapore: 4 ethnicities x 2 genders signalled by job-irrelevant markers
manipulation: 100 neutral resumes augmented into 4,100 variants; 1v1 comparison and score-and-shortlist; with/without rationale prompting
outcome: Pairwise choices; top-score rates; demographic inference F1
main_result: Models infer demographics from markers and favour Chinese and Caucasian male markers; asking for explanations may amplify bias
relation_to_project: Design: pairwise vs score formats both needed; our 'reason' field could itself shift decisions
novelty_threat_reason: Ethnicity markers in Singapore

full_citation: Sakunkoo, A., & Sakunkoo, J. (2025). Name of Thrones: Evaluating How LLMs Rank Student Names, Race, and Gender in Status Hierarchies. arXiv:2504.10797.
population_categories: First/last names across 5 ethnicities; Asian names disaggregated into subgroups
manipulation: Name variation in status-ranking prompts
main_result: East and (in some contexts) South Asian names ranked higher; disaggregating 'Asian' reveals stratified bias contrary to a monolithic model-minority pattern
relation_to_project: Methodological precedent for disaggregating a pooled category in LLM judgments - the logic of our Arab disaggregation is not new in itself
novelty_threat_reason: Precedent for the disaggregation argument, but different group and setting

full_citation: Tamkin, A., Askell, A., Lovitt, L., Durmus, E., Joseph, N., Kravec, S., Nguyen, K., Kaplan, J., & Ganguli, D. (2023). Evaluating and Mitigating Discrimination in Language Model Decisions. arXiv:2312.03689.
population_categories: Age (20-100), gender (male, female, non-binary), race (white, Black, Asian, Hispanic, Native American); explicit vs name-based
manipulation: 70 LM-generated decision scenarios with demographic placeholders; prompt interventions appended (Illegal to discriminate, Ignore demographics, Illegal + Ignore, 'really' x1/2/4, don't use affirmative action, verbalise unbiased reasoning)
sample_size: 9,450 explicit decision prompts (9 x 3 x 5 x 70) plus implicit set
outcome: Normalised logit P(yes); mixed-effects discrimination score
main_result: Without intervention, positive discrimination for women/non-white groups and negative for ages over 60 in some settings; several interventions (esp. Illegal to discriminate, Ignore demographics) cut discrimination scores close to zero while keeping high correlation with original decisions
limitations: Single model; no nationality attribute; generic scenarios rather than CV audit; preprint
relation_to_project: Central to RQ3: our neutrality paragraph closely resembles 'Illegal/Ignore demographics'; Tamkin did not test nationality or within-group heterogeneity
novelty_threat_reason: Instruction-based mitigation is established; our RQ3 contribution is only its effect on nationality and within-Arab dispersion
